claims.text: The initial sub-5 nm AuCoCuNiPt nanoparticles are single-phase FCC.
The initial nanoparticles include elliptical and icosahedral geometries.
The nanoparticles were synthesized by pulsed laser deposition on a silicon nitride membrane.
Above approximately 0.45 Tm, surface-energy effects override sluggish diffusion in sub-5 nm AuCoCuNiPt nanoparticles.
Surface-energy minimization drives Au and Cu atoms to migrate rapidly to nanoparticle surfaces.
The elemental surface energies follow the ordering γ_Au < γ_Cu < γ_Ni < γ_Co < γ_Pt.
Au and Cu segregation creates a core-shell-like composition gradient.
The core-shell-like composition gradient lowers the activation energy for surface diffusion and evaporation.
Above the critical temperature, the surface free-energy driving force exceeds the kinetic barrier associated with lattice distortion.
Surface-enriched Au and Cu evaporate because they have lower cohesive energies than Pt, Co, and Ni.
Loss of Au and Cu leaves refractory-rich particle cores.
Surface enrichment and evaporation cause particle shrinkage and coalescence of the remaining refractory-rich cores.
Evaporation of surface-enriched species promotes subsequent Ostwald ripening.
The rate of Au and Cu surface enrichment accelerates nonlinearly near 0.45 Tm.
Heating produces measurable mass loss from particles smaller than 5 nm.
Heating shifts the size distribution toward larger, refractory-rich particles.
Icosahedral particles lose Au and Cu faster than truncated-octahedral particles because their surface energy is higher.
The proposed surface-dominated mechanism applies only to particles smaller than 10 nm.
For particles larger than 20 nm, bulk sluggish diffusion dominates and the proposed mechanism does not apply.
Higher environmental pressure may suppress evaporation.

contradictions.description: The proposed mechanism requires lowered barriers and rapid Au/Cu surface diffusion, but the experiment proposes artificially enforcing high diffusion barriers while still allowing surface-energy minimization and treats persistence of the process under suppressed diffusion as a relevant confirming result. Surface segregation itself requires atomic transport, so the constrained simulation does not cleanly implement the stated mechanism.

The focal hypothesis asserts that active, rapid diffusion driven by surface energy overrides sluggish diffusion, whereas one branch of the falsification rule accepts matching a diffusion-suppressed simulation. That outcome would undermine the hypothesis's claimed need for rapid atomic migration rather than simply validate it.
